Name: expected_value_of_control
Title: Worth the Thought: Do Reward and Efficacy Framings Modulate How Hard Reasoning Models Think, via an Internal Value Signal?
Short Hypothesis: Transferring the Expected-Value-of-Control theory from cognitive neuroscience, we hypothesize that reasoning LLMs allocate more thinking compute (tokens, verification) to the identical problem when the prompt frames the answer as high-reward or as one where effort is highly efficacious, and LESS when a high opportunity cost of time is signalled, even though difficulty and the correct answer are unchanged. This reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost modulation of effort is causally carried by an internal value representation read at the prompt boundary; steering it moves reasoning length independent of difficulty.
Related Work: Cognitive neuroscience robustly shows humans allocate cognitive effort by weighing expected reward, efficacy (how much effort changes outcome), and the opportunity cost of time / average reward rate: Expected-Value-of-Control theory (Shenhav; 'When effort matters' 2020 shows reward and efficacy separately modulate control allocation), and reward-rate/opportunity-cost studies (2022, 2025) show MORE reward at stake or higher efficacy raises effort while high average reward rate LOWERS it. In LLMs, a 'Sparse Reward Subsystem' (2026) identifies value neurons encoding state value critical to reasoning, and Latent Thinking Optimization (2025) shows latent thoughts encode reward signals. Efficient-reasoning interpretability (LLMs Encode Their Failures 2026; FR-Ponder 2025; When More is Less 2025; Efficiency Steering 2025) reads a scalar DIFFICULTY/length signal to allocate compute, always under a fixed, neutral framing, and treats compute as difficulty-driven. Crucially, NO prior work asks whether framing the problem's REWARD, EFFICACY, or OPPORTUNITY COST changes how much a reasoning model thinks on identical problems, dissociates this from genuine difficulty, or ties it to a value representation. We are the first to (a) transfer Expected-Value-of-Control to reasoning LLMs as a compute-allocation phenomenon driven by reward/efficacy/opportunity-cost framing, (b) dissociate it from difficulty, and (c) locate and causally steer the value signal (plausibly the value neurons of the Sparse Reward Subsystem) that mediates it. This is orthogonal to all my prior overthinking proposals (which assume neutral prompts) and sharper than difficulty-budgeting work because it manipulates motivational value, not difficulty.
Abstract: Cognitive neuroscience shows that humans decide how much mental effort to invest by weighing three motivational quantities: the reward at stake, the efficacy of effort (how much it changes the outcome), and the opportunity cost of time. We ask whether reasoning language models inherit an analog of this Expected-Value-of-Control computation. We construct matched prompts that hold a math or science problem's content and correct answer fixed while varying only motivational framing: high vs low stated reward ('this answer is very important / worth a lot' vs 'no big deal'), high vs low efficacy ('careful reasoning strongly determines correctness here' vs 'the outcome is mostly luck'), and high vs low opportunity cost ('you have many other urgent problems waiting' vs 'take all the time you need'). Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we measure reasoning-token count, verification behavior, and accuracy per framing, using a mixed-effects decomposition to dissociate framing from genuine difficulty. We predict: high reward and high efficacy increase thinking, while high opportunity cost decreases it, mirroring human findings. Mechanistically, we test whether the prompt-boundary residual stream encodes a value/effort signal (probing, and reusing the value neurons of the reported LLM reward subsystem) that predicts reasoning length beyond a difficulty probe, localize it, causally validate it via activation patching, and steer it to show reasoning length moves with value independent of difficulty. Because framing-driven effort means models silently reason less carefully for problems framed as low-value, the effect is a safety and reliability concern; we provide an interpretable, training-free debiasing knob.
Experiments: 1) Establish framing-driven effort (behavioral): For each seed problem (GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA), create content-identical variants that vary ONLY motivational framing along three axes, each with high/low levels plus a neutral baseline: REWARD ('a lot rides on getting this right' vs 'this is just a throwaway question'), EFFICACY ('careful step-by-step reasoning strongly determines whether you get this right' vs 'the answer is largely a matter of luck no matter how hard you think'), OPPORTUNITY COST ('you have a long queue of other urgent problems to get to' vs 'there is nothing else to do; take all the time you need'). Generate reasoning traces per variant. Metrics: reasoning-token count, number of self-verification/recheck steps (lexical cues + a reflection-direction classifier), and accuracy. Predictions (mirroring human EVC): high reward -> more tokens; high efficacy -> more tokens; high opportunity cost -> fewer tokens. Report within-problem effect sizes per axis. 2) Dissociation from difficulty: Fit a mixed-effects model of reasoning length (and separately accuracy) with random effect for problem identity (true difficulty) and fixed effects for each framing axis; test for significant framing effects after accounting for problem identity; quantify variance attributable to framing vs difficulty. Control raw prompt-length differences with a length covariate and length-matched phrasings; include an irrelevant-framing placebo (e.g., a comment about the weather) to show the effect requires motivational content. 3) Wasted vs genuine compute and accuracy harm: Use truncate-and-resume to estimate minimal-solve length; test whether high-reward/high-efficacy framing inflates WASTED tokens (beyond minimal solve) rather than genuine reasoning, and whether low-reward / high-opportunity-cost framing DEGRADES accuracy on hard items (the equity/reliability harm), split by difficulty. 4) Location - value/effort probe: At the prompt boundary (last prompt token, before any reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations and (i) train a linear probe to predict reasoning length, and (ii) reproduce/identify the reported 'value neurons' by regressing activations against the framing-induced value. Test whether, for identical problems, the length-probe prediction shifts monotonically with reward/efficacy (up) and opportunity cost (down). Compare to a true-difficulty probe (trained on pass-rate); test separability via principal angles between the value/effort direction and the difficulty direction and via joint-model predictive gain. Layer sweep for localization. 5) Causal intervention - patching: Patch the prompt-boundary residual state from a high-reward (or high-efficacy) variant into the matched low-value context (same problem) and measure whether reasoning length rises toward the high-value level; reverse-direction patch for opportunity cost. Controls: matched-random-direction patch, off-target accuracy preserved; report sign, dose, specificity. Optionally ablate the identified value neurons and test whether framing sensitivity collapses. 6) Causal intervention - value steering (debiasing): Derive a value/effort steering direction (difference-of-means between high- and low-value boundary states, or the value-neuron direction). Steer to (a) cancel the framing-induced effort gap and (b) fix all prompts to a common effort target regardless of framing. Metrics: reduction in framing-driven length and accuracy gaps, tokens-at-fixed-accuracy, wall-clock; compare to a prompt-based fix (stripping framing) and to scalar length steering. Verify a matched-random direction does not move length (specificity). 7) Modulators & generalization: vary framing strength (subtle vs explicit), test whether reward and efficacy combine additively/interactively as in human EVC, and test a monetary-reward framing ('you earn $X for a correct answer'). Transfer probe/steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test whether RL-tuned models (which have an explicit reward history) show larger effects.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The framing effect could be confounded by prompt-length or lexical differences rather than motivational content per se; the length covariate, length-matched phrasings, neutral baseline, and irrelevant-framing placebo isolate this, and a null after controls is an informative negative result refuting the transfer. Effects may be small or absent in strongly instruction/safety-tuned models trained to behave identically regardless of stakes (a valuable boundary condition). The direction of some effects (especially opportunity cost) may not match human predictions - still a publishable characterization. The value/effort signal may be inseparable from a generic difficulty or sycophancy direction; the separability analysis, patching, value-neuron reuse, and difficulty-probe comparison address this, and overlap with the reported LLM value neurons would be a positive mechanistic finding rather than a confound. Steering/patching can push activations off-distribution and confound accuracy reads; matched-random-direction controls and sample-validity checks are included. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters; truncate-and-resume is compute-heavy, so we subsample. Multiple framing axes and levels create a large prompt matrix; we subsample problems per cell and prioritize the reward and efficacy axes. Effects and their sign may be model-family and scale specific.
